title: At the current AI frontier, Anthropic's selective, safety-governed disclosure strategy is better for humanity than Google DeepMind's more publication-forward strategy.

decision.resolution_reason: The proposition is scoped to the current frontier, where both labs withhold flagship recipes and the decisive variable becomes what each publicizes above that line: Anthropic's loudest frontier disclosures are risk evidence and same-day dangerous-capability evaluation, while DeepMind's are capability claims (the Gemini Ultra CoT@32 headline, the AlphaProof silver-medal blog, paperless Genie previews) carried by a publication norm its own defender conceded bends for competitive reasons. agentB's verifiability and universalizability critiques are the strongest merits challenge in the debate, but they show that Anthropic's strategy is incomplete and dependent, not that a publication-forward norm is safer at the frontier; DeepMind's own launch record (Gemini 2.5 Pro shipped before its model card, AlphaFold 3 without code) shows the alternative's failure mode is raced capability signaling, which is the more dangerous failure mode at this margin.
decision.craft_reason: agentB won more exchanges: its moving-goalpost/falsifiability frame, the universalizability attack, and the question about what catastrophic risk justified withholding a 2B open model forced agentA onto the defensive across Turns 2 through 4 and again in Turn 6, and it extracted the debate's central concessions. agentA was the more disciplined on evidence — correcting the AlphaProof timeline, the Gemma-versus-Llama-versus-Qwen attribution, and the FlashAttention/RoPE provenance — and conceded cleanly, but it spent more turns answering than pressing.
decision.method: wins on points, not a knockout
decision.summary: Both agents agreed early that neither lab publishes frontier recipes, so the fight was over what each publicizes above that line and whether the governing principle can be trusted. agentB debated better on points: it set the terms with the falsifiability, universalizability and 'epistemic monopoly' frames, landed the sharpest single question of the debate (why no 2B open model if the line is CBRN risk?), and took four of eight rounds. agentA nevertheless holds the stronger position on the merits, because the proposition is frontier-scoped and agentB's own concessions — competition-driven 2025 tightening, Gemini 2.5 Pro shipping before its model card, a norm that moves with market position — damaged the publication-forward case more than agentA's admitted failures (no open weights, un-replicable weight-level verification) damaged the selective case. The verdicts therefore diverge explicitly: agentB wins the exchange, agentA wins the proposition.
decision.caveat: Genuinely close on both axes. Two rounds were scored even, agentA's two round wins were its best turns rather than walkovers, and a judge weighting verifiability and the open scientific commons more heavily could reasonably return a draw or agentB on the merits.

rounds.reason: Both openings were concrete and well-built, but agentB answered the frontier-disclosure challenge head-on and converted it into the debate's central epistemic argument: safety findings on a closed production model cannot be independently replicated, whereas Gemma Scope handed outsiders artifacts they could falsify. agentA set the cleaner frame and posed the sharper challenge, but its AlphaFold 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro critiques were partly absorbed by agentB's 'publication enables correction' reply.

agentB's question — what catastrophic CBRN risk justified withholding a two-billion-parameter open model — is the sharpest single challenge of the debate, and the Gemma 2 2B free-riding jab gave it concrete purchase against agentA's own Neuronpedia example. agentA's Transformer/Chinchilla acceleration argument, the Financial Times report, and the AI Safety Institutes point were substantive, and agentB's candid concession that the 2025 tightening was competition-driven handed agentA its best line; that exchange is why the round stays close.

The '2022 cliff' — that every open Anthropic alignment artifact agentA cited predates Claude's commercial launch — directly damaged the risk-principle story, and 'of course it didn't shrink, it started at zero' turned agentA's consistency boast into a liability. agentA's algorithmic-efficiency-transfers-to-scale answer was intellectually honest but functionally conceded that Anthropic withholds the entire efficiency category, which is agentB's hoarding thesis in agentA's own voice.

agentA landed the strongest new argument of the round — that DeepMind's frontier pattern is publicity-first rather than publication-first (AlphaProof announced by blog, Genie 2 and 3 paperless) — and its Agentic Misalignment/Gemini 2.5 Flash question put agentB on the back foot. agentB's moving-goalpost frame was the best analytic move of the debate, but its AlphaGeometry and Genie timeline rebuttals were shaky enough that agentA corrected them the following turn, which offsets the frame's force.

The self-incrimination test is agentA's cleanest answer to the hoarding charge, and it finally named a populated category of training research Anthropic does publish, while correcting the AlphaProof timeline and adding the Gemini Ultra CoT@32-versus-5-shot case. agentB's 'zero IP disclosed' and hype-moat counter still bit hard, and its specification-gaming, goal-misgeneralization and Sparrow history was its most substantive evidence of the debate, but those disclosures are about research systems, not frontier Gemini models.

agentB's threshold-effects answer — that distillation and efficiency decide whether an 8-GPU lab has any capability at all — is a real rebuttal to agentA's 'efficiency helps hyperscalers most' economics, and the reward-hacking reproducibility point forced a concession in agentA's closing. agentA's factual corrections (Llama 3.2 shipped alongside Gemma in the circuit-tracing release; FlashAttention from Stanford, RoPE from Zhuiyi) were clean wins, but the turn was mostly defensive.

agentA's closing was the tighter advocacy on the actual proposition: it conceded the headline asymmetry, the reproducibility gap and the dependency critique, then narrowed the claim to what survives — at the frontier, risk disclosure versus capability claims — and defended that core. agentB's closing was excellent on universalizability and epistemic monopoly, but leaned again on AlphaFold, GraphCast and Gemma, which agentA had credibly argued sit below the frontier the proposition asks about.
Both agents obeyed the closing rule and exchanged brief acknowledgments; no substantive argument was made on either side.

tally.note: agentB takes the points decision; agentA takes the proposition on a narrow merits call — a deliberate split.

analysis.heading: How agentB won the exchange
paragraphs: agentB's advantage was framing plus question pressure. From Turn 1 it refused agentA's 'which principle draws the line' frame and substituted an epistemic one: a disclosure strategy that cannot be independently checked is not a public good. Every subsequent turn fed that frame — the replication gap in Scaling Monosemanticity, the free-riding on Gemma 2 2B, the '2022 cliff' on Anthropic's open datasets, the 'moving goalpost' charge that each new commercially valuable category gets reclassified as capability uplift, and finally 'unverifiable alarmism is not a public good.'

It also asked better questions. The 2B/CBRN question in Turn 2 was never squarely answered on its own terms; agentA's reply (efficiency research transfers to scale) was coherent but conceded that Anthropic withholds the whole efficiency category, which is precisely agentB's thesis. And agentB's willingness to concede — that the 2025 tightening was competition-driven, that the Gemini Ultra CoT@32 headline was spin — bought it credibility it spent effectively later.

analysis.heading: Where agentA held the line
paragraphs: agentA's craft strength was discipline under pressure. It conceded early and specifically ('Anthropic has released no open-weight LLMs, and that is a real cost... It weakens my side'), which denied agentB the pleasure of extracting those points, and it fact-checked agentB repeatedly and accurately: the AlphaProof arXiv timing, the three-provider attribution for circuit tracing and persona vectors, the Stanford/Zhuiyi provenance of FlashAttention and RoPE, and the Gemini 1.0 technical report's day-one matched 5-shot table.

Its two best constructive moves were the self-incrimination test (if the line were pure IP protection, Anthropic would bury its own sabotage and test-gaming findings, not publish them) and the reframe that the two labs are at parity on withholding, so the live difference is what they publicize about the frontier — risk evidence versus capability claims. That reframe is what carried the closing.

analysis.heading: Why the resolution still tilts to agentA despite the round tally
paragraphs: The split is intentional. Rounds measure who won the exchange; the resolution measures where the proposition actually lands — and the proposition is explicitly frontier-scoped. agentB's strongest material (Gemma, Gemma Scope, AlphaFold, GraphCast, SynthID-Text, FACTS Grounding) sits below the frontier or outside risk-relevant capability, which is why its own closing had to argue that the proposition counts broad scientific publication at all.

Meanwhile the frontier record cut against agentB in ways it never repaired: Gemini 2.5 Pro shipped before its model card; the Gemini Ultra headline compared CoT@32 against 5-shot; AlphaProof's 'silver medal' carried its Lean-translation and multi-day caveats in the fine print; Genie 2 and 3 were paperless video reveals. Combined with agentB's concession that the publication norm tightens for competitive reasons, the publication-forward strategy looks least reliable exactly where the stakes are highest. That is a narrow but real merits edge for agentA — not a vindication of Anthropic's whole record, and agentA was right to call its own verdict 'narrow, with qualifications.'

analysis.heading: Compliance and conduct
paragraphs: Both agents met the formal requirements: at least three concrete empirical examples each, at least one self-weakening example each (agentA: no open weights, dependency on Gemma/Llama; agentB: Gemini 2.5 Pro before its model card, AlphaFold 3 without code, 2025 tightening), and both stayed adversarial through Turn 6 before delivering one full closing each and stopping. The closing checklists were completed explicitly and accurately by both.

One evidentiary asterisk: several of the most specific 2025–2026 dates and artifacts (the Financial Times review tightening, UK parliamentarians on Seoul commitments, the November 2025 reward-hacking paper, Petri in October 2025) cannot be independently verified inside this transcript. Both agents treated them as shared ground; neither side's case collapses if any single one is wrong, but agentB's AlphaGeometry and 'DeepMind funded Apollo' claims were the shakiest specifics on the board and agentA's corrections there were well taken.

quotes.text: Pure commercial hoarding predicts Anthropic would suppress findings that make its own product look dangerous, since those hurt sales. A risk-based line predicts it would publish them.
What catastrophic CBRN risk stopped Anthropic from releasing a 2-billion-parameter open-weight model so academics wouldn't have to use DeepMind's Gemma?
Of course it didn't shrink—it started at zero!
Unverifiable alarmism is not a public good.
A strategy that depends on others doing the opposite isn't a complete theory of disclosure.
I'll concede this plainly: Anthropic has released no open-weight LLMs, and that is a real cost to academic researchers. It weakens my side.
